Ortigia, 22nd September. A year after their honeymoon, Matei, Giulia and four-month-old Viola arrive at Signora Concetta's B&B. Tomorrow the restoration of the Caravaggio begins.
Welcome back, you two! At last! And who is this little princess?
This is Viola. She left Sorrento this morning and slept the whole way, even on the ferry.
Having slept so much, she won't let you get a wink of sleep tonight. I know, I brought up four.
And the suitcase arrived this time! Since we came by car, we kept an eye on it for nine hundred kilometres.
(laughs) Knowing you, I knew you'd be back. I've got the same room ready for you, with the lemon.
Thank you, Signora Concetta. Once we've put Viola to bed, could we have dinner on the terrace?
Of course. I've made pasta with sardines. And tomorrow morning, once you've had breakfast, go straight to the church: someone is waiting for you.
A gentleman from Florence, who arrived last night. Very elegant, with his hands behind his back. He asked whether the church was warm enough. His name is… Bellini.
Bellini? But he said he was too old for cold churches!
Evidently, once he heard about the baby, he changed his mind. Men only change their minds for two things: a painting or a baby. He, poor man, has both.

GH = a hard "g", double TT: tra-GET-to.
GG + I = a long "j", the "i" isn't pronounced: pon-TEJ-jo.
In written or careful style, "after doing X" can be said with just the PAST PARTICIPLE at the start. It's very elegant and short:
After breakfast, go to the church.
Saputo della bambina, ha cambiato idea.
On hearing about the baby, he changed his mind.
English has something similar: "The work finished, we went out." "Once home, we had dinner."
The participle agrees with the OBJECT (for verbs with avere) or with the SUBJECT (for verbs with essere):
Don't forget the agreement: "Finita la cena", NOT "Finito la cena". "Fatte le valigie", NOT "Fatto le valigie" (in careful style).
As with the imperative and the infinitive, pronouns attach to the end of the absolute participle:
Having said goodbye to them, he left.
As soon as he saw her, he recognised her.
Once we'd put Viola to bed, we had dinner.
4. The past gerund: avendo / essendo + participle
The past gerund shows an action COMPLETED before another, often with a sense of CAUSE ("because / since…"):
Avendo dormito tanto, stanotte non dormirà.
Having slept so much, she won't sleep tonight.
Essendo partiti in macchina, abbiamo portato tutto.
Essendo arrivata tardi, Giulia non ha cenato.
Having arrived late, Giulia didn't have dinner.
Pronouns attach to "avendo / essendo": "Avendolo visto, ho capito." "Essendosi svegliata presto, era stanca."

On the twentieth of September, exactly a year after the wedding, Matei and Giulia went back to the church of Sant'Antonino in Sorrento. This time there were no three hundred guests, no tarantella, no pălincă from Ion. There were just the two of them, Viola in the baby carrier and Grandma Assunta, who, having celebrated her birthday the week before, had decided that at a certain age you can go to church on a Tuesday too.

Sitting in the same pew where they had exchanged rings, they stayed silent for a while. "A year," Giulia said softly. "It feels like ten have gone by." "Or ten minutes," replied Matei. Assunta, who heard everything, muttered: "Wait till you get to seventy. Then it'll feel like yesterday." Then she took Viola in her arms and sang her a Neapolitan song so old that nobody knew the words any more.

The next day, having said goodbye to the family, they set off south by car. Having loaded everything they needed for six months, the little Fiat looked like a removal lorry: suitcases, pram, travel cot, brushes, solvents and, strapped into the back seat like a passenger, Totò. "We couldn't leave him with Graziella for six months," Giulia had said. "He'd have felt abandoned."

Once at Villa San Giovanni, they took the ferry to Messina. It was the first time Viola had seen the sea. Matei took her up on deck in the carrier and showed her the waves, the seagulls, the coast of Sicily drawing closer. Viola looked at everything with her usual seriousness, then reached out a hand towards the wind, as if she wanted to touch it. "She's Neapolitan," said Giulia. "The sea is in her blood." "She's Romanian too," said Matei. "You'll see, she'll love the mountains."

Signora Concetta was waiting for them at the door of the B&B, in an apron covered in flour. As soon as she saw Viola, she completely forgot about Matei and Giulia. She took her in her arms, carried her into the kitchen and introduced her to every lemon in the house, one by one, as if they were relatives. Totò, meanwhile, was settled on the balcony, next to the biggest lemon tree, so that he wouldn't feel lonely. That evening, once the baby was in bed, they had dinner on the terrace, as they had a year before. The rule this time was different: "No rules," Giulia had said. "Except one: whoever wakes up first makes the coffee."

The next morning, after breakfast, they went to the church of Santa Lucia alla Badia. In front of Caravaggio's great painting the scaffolding was already up, six metres high, with the lamps and microscopes. And at the foot of the scaffolding, with his hands behind his back, in a coat far too heavy for Sicily in September, stood Professor Bellini.

"Professor!" exclaimed Giulia. "But you said cold churches…" "I've said a lot of things, Esposito," he interrupted. "But on hearing that the baby would be coming to Sicily, I thought someone ought to make sure nobody taught her bad habits. Touching paintings, for example." Then he bent down towards the carrier. "Good morning, Signorina Viola. Welcome to work."

Then Bellini did something neither of them expected. He took an envelope out of his pocket and handed it to Matei. "I wrote it last night, having arrived before you," he said. "But read it later. Once the first day's work is over." Matei put it in his pocket, next to Ernesto's brush, without asking any questions. He had learned that with Bellini questions were no use.

They climbed the scaffolding, he on one side, she on the other. Viola stayed down below in her pram, next to the professor, who explained to her in a low voice, as if to a colleague, the composition of the painting: the gravediggers in the foreground, the saint on the ground, the crowd behind, and above it all the great dark void that Caravaggio had left on purpose. "The void," he told her, "is the hardest part to paint. And to restore."

Matei picked up Ernesto's tiny brush. Giulia looked at him from the other side of the scaffolding and nodded. He touched the painting for the first time, in a corner at the bottom left, the one they had noticed together a year before, sitting on the pew, without saying a word. A tiny brushstroke, almost invisible. From below, Bellini whispered to Viola: "Look. Your father has just begun the most important work of his life."

That evening, back at Concetta's, once Viola was in bed, they opened the envelope on the terrace among the lemon trees. Inside was a handwritten sheet, in the professor's elegant hand. "Dear Matei and Giulia, once this restoration is finished, I shall retire. I am sixty-two and I have a grandfather watching me from a photograph. From next September, the two of you will run the workshop. This is not a proposal. It is a decision. Ernesto would agree."

Under the signature there was one last line, smaller, almost shy: "P.S. If the little one, as she grows up, should want to become a restorer, I would be happy to teach her the first rule. Having already told it to the two of you, I believe I still know it by heart." Giulia passed the sheet to Matei. Neither of them spoke. Above them, over the sea at Ortigia, the first stars were coming out.
